Lessons.Title: Representations of Fractions (Part 2)
ExplanationParagraphs: Original 2021 Grade4 Unit2 Lesson2: interpret non-unit fractions from one or more equal-length wholes. Source teacher lesson and original three-page Student Task Statements, including A–O bars and improper fractions, inspected visually. Existing introduction/goal kept.

Warm-up Which One Doesn't Belong (10 min): original source figures A–D. A one shaded part can represent1/4, B and D can represent1/3; C has unequal parts and cannot be called1/3. Open interpretations remain teacher-reviewed.

Activity1 A Diagram for Each Fraction (20 min): match all fifteen original fractions to A–M: A4/8, B2/3, C3/5, D7/8, E6/10, F5/6, G3/8, H4/6, I2/5, J3/4, K4/10, L6/12, M5/12. The two fractions with NO diagram are6/6 and7/10; learner constructs new source-appropriate N and O representations, teacher reviews equal partitions.
Discuss original equal shaded lengths despite unlike denominators: A and L (4/8=6/12), B and H (2/3=4/6), C and E (3/5=6/10), I and K (2/5=4/10). Compare using the SAME whole length.

Activity2 Diagrams for Some Other Fractions (15 min): source p3 a1/2,b3/2,c4/3,d4/4,e6/4. Fractions greater than one require two or more unit-whole sections. Students also draw and shade2/2,4/2,5/4,10/8 with equal parts and correct whole markers; teacher assesses diagrams.

Lesson synthesis (10 min): a/b counts a unit parts each 1/b of a whole; some counts exceed one and equivalent fractions name the same area. Original source paper strips saved from preceding lesson may support representation.

Edulytics first-party five-minute Cool-down, NOT publisher's educator-gated original: draw5/4 across two wholes and justify4/8=6/12 with equal-whole fraction bars. Teacher reviews drawings; existing Practice numeric items supplement but do not auto-grade complete art/source image tasks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Non-unit fraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: a copies of a unit fraction1/b.
KeyConcepts.Rule: a/b is a equal pieces each of size1/b.

KeyConcepts.Title: Improper fraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: Fraction with numerator at least denominator, using as many wholes as needed.
KeyConcepts.Example: 3/2 is one whole plus one half.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent shaded areas
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different numerator/denominator names for the same share of a fixed whole.
KeyConcepts.Example: B and H represent equal shaded shares.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source A–M mapping
WorkedExamples.Question: What do the original shaded bars represent?
WorkedExamples.Method: Count equal divisions and shaded parts.
Steps: Read1 whole as total length of each source bar.
Identify6/6 and7/10 as the two unmatched fractions, then draw them.

WorkedExamples.Title: Improper fractions
WorkedExamples.Question: How should5/4 be shown?
WorkedExamples.Method: One full unit whole and another quarter.
Steps: Divide an equal-size second whole into4.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independently authored Grade 4 lesson reasoning
WorkedExamples.Question: How many wholes and fourths does 7/4 represent?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the exact relationship and representation requested by this lesson.
Steps: Regroup to 1 3/4 of the same-sized whole.
WorkedExamples.Check: First-party mathematically checked model. Original publisher activity and student drawings require independent teacher review.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Clamping improper fraction shading to one whole.
Treating unequal partition areas as equal fraction parts.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The denominator assumes equal-size unit parts.

SummaryPoints: 2021 source p2 has fifteen fraction labels, A–M displayed and N/O blanks;6/6 and7/10 require constructed bars.
Original A–D warm-up and all open explanations remain teacher-reviewed; digital numerics only supplementary.
Equivalent area examples A/L,B/H,C/E,I/K require same-size whole.
